941: D and E are correct because IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) work by defining an IAM role with the permissions the Kubernetes service account needs (D) and annotating the Kubernetes service account with that role's Amazon Resource Name (ARN), so EKS automatically injects temporary AWS credentials only into pods that use that service account. E is correct because the IAM role must have a trust relationship with an OpenID Connect identity provider created from the EKS cluster's OIDC issuer URL, which lets IAM validate and trust the service account tokens issued by the cluster. Together these two steps give each service account secure, granular, least-privilege access to specific AWS resources instead of sharing the broad node instance role.
942: C is correct because SSE-KMS uses the AWS managed key (aws/s3), which AWS automatically rotates every year at no additional key charge, satisfying the annual rotation requirement while minimizing the cost of the encryption key. Every use of the KMS key to encrypt or decrypt objects is logged as an API call in AWS CloudTrail, so key usage and rotation activity can be audited. Customer managed KMS keys incur an additional monthly charge per key, and SSE-S3 and SSE-C do not provide both automatic annual rotation tracking and CloudTrail visibility.
943: C is correct because tagging all resources with a cost key whose value is the application name, and then activating those tags as cost allocation tags, causes AWS to break down and group spending by application in the billing data. Cost Explorer can then display the per-application breakdown and be configured to deliver regularly scheduled reports, all with no additional infrastructure or licensing cost. Standing up an RDS instance to query raw Cost and Usage Reports adds unnecessary cost and operational overhead.
944: B is correct because running the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones protects the web tier from the failure of any single AZ and lets capacity recover automatically, while a Multi-AZ RDS deployment maintains a synchronous standby replica in another AZ for automatic database failover. Amazon CloudFront serves the static assets from S3 through its global edge network, adding resilience and performance for the static content. The single-AZ designs leave a single point of failure, and EFS One Zone storage does not match S3 plus a CDN for resilient static asset delivery.
945: C is correct because a Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built to distribute traffic to third-party security appliances for inline traffic inspection, and the GenerateGatewayLoadBalancer endpoint is an interface endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink that lets application accounts send cross-account traffic to the appliance privately. Deploying the GWLB in the networking account centralizes the security appliance while all traffic between accounts stays on the AWS private network. ALBs, NLBs, and plain interface endpoints cannot perform the transparent inline inspection and traffic flow cloning that GWLB provides.
946: A is correct because an Aurora custom endpoint is a user-defined endpoint whose member instances you control, so a custom endpoint can include only the three Aurora Replicas with the larger compute and memory specification. Pointing the department's reporting queries at the custom endpoint automatically load balances those queries across exactly those three instances while keeping the workload isolated from the rest of the cluster. The reader endpoint would spread the load across all six replicas, and individual instance endpoints provide no load balancing.
947: B is correct because AWS Secrets Manager is designed to store database credentials and supports automatic rotation of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL credentials on a schedule such as every 30 days with native, built-in rotation support, so no custom rotation code is needed. The Lambda function simply calls the Secrets Manager API to retrieve the current credentials at runtime, eliminating the connection string stored in an environment variable. Parameter Store would require writing a custom rotation Lambda function, and encrypted environment variables and KMS keys provide no managed credential rotation at all.
948: B is correct because an AWS DMS serverless replication task automatically provisions and scales the replication capacity it needs based on the actual workload, allocating only the capacity required as the amount of data to replicate varies throughout the day. This removes the need to size and pay for a fixed replication instance that must handle peak volumes. Multi-AZ replication, EC2 Auto Scaling, and ECS with Fargate are not valid mechanisms for scaling DMS capacity.
949: D is correct because AWS PrivateLink creates a private connection between the application VPC and the third-party SaaS application hosted on AWS by using interface endpoints, so traffic flows over the Amazon private network instead of the public internet. This provides secure, private connectivity with minimal public internet exposure while the SaaS provider retains control of its endpoint. VPN and Transit Gateway routing still traverse the public internet or add unnecessary network complexity compared with PrivateLink.
950: C is correct because an AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates IPsec tunnels that encrypt all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC at the network layer, and the tunnel's session security associations provide session-layer encryption, while route tables, security groups, and network ACLs restrict access to only the required traffic. Direct Connect by itself provides no encryption in transit, and IAM policies control console and API access rather than network connectivity. This combination satisfies both the encryption and the access-control requirements.
951: C is correct because AWS Secrets Manager securely stores the RDS for MySQL credentials and lets the application retrieve them with a simple API call, eliminating the embedded credentials with minimal programming effort. A Lambda rotation function scheduled by Secrets Manager rotates the credentials automatically on the configured schedule without manual intervention. KMS is a key management service not intended for storing application credentials, local storage keeps the secrets on the host, and Parameter Store has no native rotation scheduling for database credentials.
952: C is correct because Cross-Region Replication on the existing S3 bucket automatically and asynchronously copies objects to a bucket in another AWS Region, and SSE-S3 encrypts every object at rest with keys managed entirely by Amazon S3 at no additional cost and no key administration. Amazon Athena then analyzes the existing and new data with standard SQL directly against the objects in S3, requiring no servers or data loads to manage, which keeps operational overhead minimal. Multi-Region KMS keys add cost and management overhead, and loading data into RDS for querying creates significant extra work.
953: A is correct because the uploaded images are only needed for AI model training twice a year, so S3 Glacier Deep Archive provides the lowest possible storage cost even accounting for two retrievals per year. Premium users can download generated images at any time, so those images belong in S3 Standard for immediate, frequent access. Non-premium users can only download once every 6 hours, an infrequent access pattern that S3 Standard-IA serves with immediate availability at a lower storage price. This tiering matches each dataset's access pattern to its cheapest suitable storage class.
954: D is correct because the SQS queue buffers asynchronous requests and smooths out bursts of thousands of requests, and ECS services can be configured to read from the queue while auto scaling adjusts both the cluster capacity and the number of service tasks based on queue depth. Each ML microservice runs as a long-running container that loads its 1 GB of model data from S3 once at startup and keeps it in memory, avoiding the repeated cold-start and memory-loading penalty that Lambda functions would incur each time an idle model is invoked. ECS with SQS-driven scaling therefore fits the irregular usage patterns across hundreds of users far better than a request-driven function model.
955: A is correct because it builds a pilot-light DR in the second Region where the ALB and Auto Scaling group exist but run at minimum capacity, so the standby environment costs almost nothing while the primary is healthy yet can scale up within the 30-minute recovery objective when needed. Converting the cluster to an Aurora global database keeps the data continuously replicated to the secondary Region, and Route 53 active-passive failover switches user traffic to the DR ALB endpoints when the primary Region fails. This meets the requirement that the DR site does not need to serve customers while the primary infrastructure is healthy.
956: D is correct because the batch jobs cannot be disrupted, and EC2 On-Demand Instances provide uninterrupted capacity without the two-minute interruption notice risk that Spot Instances carry. Storing the generated data in S3 Standard during the 30-day access period and then transitioning it to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for the remainder of the 2-year retention minimizes storage cost, and an S3 lifecycle expiration rule deletes the data automatically after 2 years. This combination keeps both compute and storage costs as low as possible while meeting the disruption and retention requirements.
957: B and D are correct because D establishes an AWS Direct Connect connection with a transit virtual interface to a Direct Connect gateway, providing the dedicated private connectivity with the consistent low single-digit millisecond latency that hybrid workloads require. B associates that Direct Connect gateway with the transit gateway already attached to the VPCs, so every VPC connected to the transit gateway can reach the on-premises data center through the single Direct Connect connection. This is the most cost-effective design because one private connection serves all VPCs, whereas Site-to-Site VPN connections add per-tunnel cost and cannot guarantee single-digit latency.
958: A is correct because Amazon RDS Proxy sits between the application and the RDS for PostgreSQL instance, pooling database connections and, during a Multi-AZ failover, automatically detecting the new primary and reconnecting pooled connections to it, which sharply reduces the timeout errors applications experience during failovers. Applications connect through the proxy endpoint, so they are shielded from DNS propagation delays and connection storms after failover. Read replicas, monitoring, and snapshots do not shorten failover time for the production writer endpoint.
959: C is correct because AWS Systems Manager State Manager associations enforce a desired state on a defined schedule, so associations can automatically stop the tagged development RDS instances after business hours and start them again before business hours without any custom code. State Manager can target the instances by their existing development tags, and the schedule runs reliably every business day, giving the least operational overhead. EventBridge with Lambda would require writing and maintaining functions, and CloudWatch alarms and Trusted Advisor are detection tools rather than schedulers.
960: A is correct because the Requester Pays feature makes the marketing firm's AWS account pay the data transfer and request costs whenever it downloads data from the bucket, which minimizes the survey company's data transfer costs as the firm in the new geographic region consumes the data. The data remains in a single bucket with no replication or duplicate storage charges, and access is still governed by bucket policies. Cross-Region Replication would double storage and add replication transfer costs, and RAM sharing or Intelligent-Tiering do not shift or reduce data transfer costs.
